items.text: SEASON 9 · EPISODE 4 · DRAFT · CASE-048  The lobby and the MER · Maya, Raffa (IT director and network owner), Tamsin and Kit · Level L5 · Advanced support (formulas on request)  On full nights, paging comes out in pieces. The one voice a full lobby must be able to hear shares its path with nine hundred phones.  ⚑ RV-170: the network is Raffa’s; what paging says in an incident is the duty manager’s. RV-172: figures illustrative. Some choices run on a clock.

items.title: The Paging Path
items.stakes: On full nights, paging breaks up. If the duty manager has to tell a full lobby to stay where it is, nobody knows whether they'll hear her.
items.reward: A paging path nothing else can crowd out — proven on a full night.

objectives.text: Find who paging shares its path with

items.alt: The lobby during a charity livestream, crowded with guests watching phones; broken words float from the ceiling; Tamsin at the paging microphone points up; Maya looks up.

bubbles.text: That was me saying ‘please take your seats’.
Every guest is on the Wi-Fi.

items.caption: A charity stream, a full lobby.

lines.text: If I ever have to say ‘stay where you are’ to a full lobby, I need them to hear every word.
Then we find out what paging is sharing its path with.

items.text: Act I — “Same VLAN as the guests”

items.prompt: 21:45. Paging is breaking up. What do you check first?
items.risk: A full lobby that can't hear ‘stay where you are’.

hints.text: What does a life-safety voice depend on — and what does paging share?

options.label: First that the fire alarm's voice evacuation is separate and unaffected; then ask Raffa for the lobby switch's VLAN map and tonight's uplink graph
options.result: Voice evacuation: separate, unaffected. The map: paging on VLAN 20 with the guest access points. The uplink: 108%.
options.consequence: The life-safety path first, then measure the path.

options.label: Move the paging stations to a spare port yourself
options.consequence: Changes a network that isn't yours.
options.fail: The network belongs to its owner.

options.label: Replace the paging microphone
options.result: A new microphone, broken the same way.
options.consequence: The wrong end of the path.

items.title: Same VLAN as the guests.
items.body: Raffa's map says it plainly. During last spring's lobby expansion the two paging stations and the DSP's paging input were moved onto VLAN 20 — the same segment as the new guest access points — with a note: ‘for now — revisit’. Tonight about 900 guests pull roughly 1.2 Mb/s each: 1,080 Mb/s through a 1,000 Mb/s uplink. At 108%, the switch drops packets. It doesn't ask whose.
items.label: Test: the utilization — and why paging was there.

items.sub: Advanced · the skill behind this chapter

items.alt: A teaching moment: Raffa and Maya beside a board. Nine hundred guests on the Wi-Fi at about one point two megabits each, all on the lobby uplink. One thousand and eighty megabits on a one-gigabit link — a hundred and eight percent. Paging shares that VLAN. Then paging gets its own VLAN and its own queue. My switches, my change — tonight's window.

bubbles.text: Nine hundred guests on the Wi-Fi at about one point two megabits each, all on the lobby uplink.

items.alt: A path sheet before the fix: two paging stations and the guest access points with 900 guests both feed one 1,000 Mb/s uplink to the DSP, all on VLAN 20; the guest line thick, the paging line dashed; 900 × 1.2 = 1,080 Mb/s; uplink at 108%, paging dropped before the DSP; the fire alarm voice evacuation separate and unaffected.
items.caption: The one voice that must get through, in a queue with nine hundred phones.

items.label: **Fix it:** give paging its own path.

items.title: Priority isn't independence.
items.body: Kit finds the reason nobody worried: the DSP gives paging priority — the program ducks the moment the paging mic opens. Everyone believed paging was protected. But priority lives inside the DSP, and the packets were being thrown away on the uplink before they got there. And the venue's emergency plan uses exactly this paging for the duty manager's ‘please stay where you are’.
items.label: Test: paging's share of the load — and whose words it carries.

items.prompt: Friday. How does the network change?
items.risk: A life-safety instruction lost in guest traffic.
timeout: Saturday's stream shares the path again.

hints.text: What should paging never have to share?

options.label: Ask for a bigger uplink
options.result: Next year's bigger stream fills that too.
options.consequence: More room in the same shared queue.

options.label: Hand Raffa the requirement — paging on its own VLAN, guests on an isolated guest VLAN with a cap, priority queuing for paging on the uplinks — his design, his change, Friday's window
options.result: Raffa builds it Friday night; the uplink will never be asked for more than it has by guests alone.
options.consequence: Separate, then prioritise — by the network's owner.

options.label: Turn the guest Wi-Fi off during shows
options.result: The charity's donors can't watch the stream they came for.
options.consequence: Breaks the event to save the page.

options.label: Tell Tamsin to shout
options.result: She will. It isn't a design.

items.title: A line for one kind of message
items.body: During the Cuban Missile Crisis in 1962, messages between Washington and Moscow could take hours to arrive, relayed through embassies and cables used for everything else. In 1963 the two governments agreed a direct link for nothing but each other's most urgent messages. It is often pictured as a red telephone; it began as a pair of teleprinters.

items.text: ✦ UX RULE #85 · AVERY'S LENS  Priority isn't independence  A message that must always get through needs its own path — not just a higher place in a queue it shares with everyone else.  Paging had priority inside the DSP. The packets were dropped before they got there, in a lobby full of guests on the same network.

items.alt: The path sheet after the fix: paging on VLAN 30 with priority, drawn thick; guests on VLAN 90, capped and isolated; the uplink at 71%, 20 of 20 test pages clean; voice evacuation still separate.
items.caption: Its own path, then priority.

items.prompt: You could've just moved the ports yourself. You've got the switch password from commissioning.

options.label: “It's your network. I'd rather hand you a clear requirement than have you find my change in a log.”
options.reply: Then I'll give you a VLAN and a queue by Friday. And I'll change that password.

items.title: VLAN 20: paging + guest APs
items.body: Raffa's VLAN map for the lobby switch: ports 1–2 paging stations, port 5 DSP paging input, ports 10–11 guest access points — all VLAN 20. A note from the expansion: ‘paging moved here for now — revisit’.

items.risk: A fix that works only when nobody's there.
timeout: The next full night is the test.

hints.text: When did it fail — and where would you listen?

options.label: Raffa's change log says it's done
At Saturday's full-lobby stream, twenty test pages from both stations, listened for in the lobby and both bars — and Tamsin told exactly what she can rely on
options.result: Twenty clean pages; the uplink at 71%; Tamsin briefs the ushers anyway.
options.consequence: Prove it on the night it failed.

options.label: Test it on Monday morning in an empty lobby
options.result: An empty lobby proves an empty lobby.

items.label: **Service Mode:** run Thursday to Saturday yourself.

items.body: The lobby uplink's graph for Thursday night: flat at 108% of its offered load from 20:55 to 21:35, with dropped packets climbing. The stream ended at 21:36. So did the paging problem.

items.text: FIELD NOTE —  Count the load on the path (% = traffic ÷ link speed × 100). Priority inside a box can’t save packets lost before they reach it: a message that must always get through needs its own path first, priority second. Hand the network owner a clear requirement — they change the network. Check life-safety systems are separate before anything else, tell the incident commander what she can rely on, and prove the fix on the kind of night it failed.
REFLECTION (optional)  · What must-get-through message in your world shares its path with everything else?
